issues.item: Avoid Public Transport: Using public transport
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Public Transport' is hard to justify from the rest of the profile. The triggers are auditory/name/voice reminders linked to childhood caregiver abuse, and the negative appraisals are shame/self-blame/meaninglessness. Avoiding public transport suggests a situational safety strategy tied to a specific external environment, but there are no threat, memory, or trigger items indicating transport-related danger, crowding, entrapment, or encounters with abuse reminders in that context. This makes the item clinically difficult to integrate with the rest of the selected profile and with the formulation, where maladaptive strategies are closely linked to triggers and appraisals.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: 'Contamination/feeling dirty' is more characteristically tied to sexual trauma and is difficult to reconcile as a central appraisal in this profile of childhood physical abuse without any supporting memory, trigger, or threat content suggesting bodily violation themes.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: Avoiding evaluation of appearance/performance fits social-evaluative shame concerns, but the rest of the profile centers childhood caregiver abuse with auditory/name/voice reminders and self-blame/meaning loss. This strategy is not well supported by the listed triggers or appraisals and feels aimed at a different symptom cluster than the rest of the profile.

vignette: Amara was eight when the man who raised her began swinging his belt not as a fleeting punishment, but as a sustained campaign of violence. It started in the hallway, but quickly moved wherever she was-kitchens, bedrooms, the narrow stairwell. What she remembers most clearly is the sharp crack against the plaster, the heavy thud of his work boots on the hardwood, and the low, rhythmic cadence of his voice as he named her faults before the blows landed. She learned to brace herself at the sound of his footsteps, to flatten her body against the wall when the front door clicked open, to hold her breath until the shouting stopped. Decades later, the memory retains that same suffocating weight. She never argued back. She just waited for it to end, and in the quiet that followed, her mind kept circling back to what he had done, replaying his movements, his words, his choices, while she sat on the edge of her bed wondering how she could have been so fundamentally broken to deserve it. Over the years, the sounds never fully faded. As a teenager and then an adult, she found herself wincing at the heavy drop of a shop vacuum, the metallic clank of a pipe wrench striking concrete, or even the way a site supervisor's voice cut through a construction yard. When a client on a service call said her name in a sharp, commanding tone, her shoulders locked instantly. She began avoiding foremen, building inspectors, and anyone in a uniform, telling herself she just preferred working solo. The avoidance started small-taking jobs from a different contractor, ducking into alleyways when a patrol car rolled slowly past her worksite-but it calcified into habit. She stopped answering calls from old acquaintances whose names echoed in her childhood hallway. Her home stayed sparse, the furniture arranged so nothing felt like his old house, yet she still caught herself scanning rooms for objects that felt off, discarding heavy leather straps, thick work boots, even certain shades of brown wood paneling when she renovated. Concurrently, her mind drifted into other-blame rumination. She would lie awake, tracing the sequence of his actions, focusing exclusively on what he had done to her. The rumination and the avoidance occupied the same days without touching each other, each simply a fact of her routine. At forty-seven, Amara works as a plumber, running service calls across the city. The job demands she be around authority figures constantly-property managers, city inspectors, clients who expect immediate answers. Every time a foreman radios over a headset with a clipped tone, or a building manager taps a clipboard against a wall, her pulse jumps and her breath shortens. She tells herself she just dislikes that type of voice. She has come to believe the abuse happened because of what she was at her core, that her own nature made her an easy target. Alongside that belief, days began to lose their weight. Her marriage, once a refuge, now feels like she is walking on glass, afraid her husband will see the defectiveness she is convinced resides in her bones. She completes the work because it is what she does, not because it matters. She runs snakes through walls and tightens fittings, but nothing in her routine feels meaningful anymore. The hollow flatness and the belief in her own defectiveness simply co-existed, filling her shifts and her evenings. Three months ago, a routine inspection turned into a confrontation that left her shaking for an hour after she fled the site. She had been called into a foreman's office, the door shut behind her, and when he asked to see her work logs, his voice dropped into the exact register she had spent a lifetime avoiding. She left her tool belt on the floor and walked out. Her husband found her sitting in the truck, gripping the steering wheel, unable to process his questions. It was then she realized she could no longer outrun the echoes. She finally made an appointment, not because she expects to be fixed, but because she is tired of bracing for a blow that is not there. What frightens her most is that the sounds will always find her, that she will never stop scanning rooms for the man who hurt her. What she hopes for, quietly, is a way to sit through a job site without her heart hammering, to hear her own name without flinching, and to believe that the flaw she saw in herself back then was never the truth.
